text: Detailed reference anatomy of the rice grain and flowering structure (Matsuo and Hoshikawa, 1993; Vergara, 1989). A rice grain (rough rice) consists of the hull (husk), the brown rice/caryopsis inside it, the rachilla, sterile lemmas, rudimentary glumes, and the pedicel connecting it to the panicle branch. The hull is made of two parts that interlock: the larger lemma and the smaller palea, joined at the ridged edges; when hulls separate at threshing this is called dehulling. The brown rice (caryopsis) consists of three main parts: the pericarp (outer bran layer) and aleurone layer (protein/nutrient-rich inner bran layer) together forming the bran that is removed during milling; the endosperm, which is the starchy interior making up roughly 90% of the grain's dry weight and the main food reserve for germination; and the embryo (germ), located at the base of the grain, containing the plumule (embryonic shoot), radicle (embryonic root), scutellum (which absorbs nutrients from the endosperm during germination), and a vascular bundle connecting these structures. The panicle (inflorescence) consists of a panicle base, a central panicle axis, primary branches emerging from the axis, secondary branches emerging from the primary branches, pedicels, and spikelets at the pedicel tips - each spikelet contains one floret in cultivated rice. Rice is self-pollinating: each floret contains both stamens (male, consisting of a filament and anther producing pollen) and a pistil (female, consisting of the stigma, style, and ovary) enclosed by the lemma and palea. After the ovary is fertilized by pollen from its own floret's anthers, it develops into the grain. Flowering/anthesis (anther dehiscence and pollination) typically occurs in the morning, between roughly 5:00 and 12:00.
